title: Provide customer service in a sales and distribution environment

lessons.title: Who our customers are and what they need
lessons.html:
Customers keep the business alive

An abattoir or meat plant sells carcasses, cuts and by-products to butcheries, retailers, wholesalers, restaurants and sometimes directly to farmers and the public. Without these customers there is no income and no jobs. Customer service is everything we do to make customers want to buy from us again.

External and internal customers

  • External customers buy from the business: a butchery owner in town, a supermarket buyer, a farmer bringing cattle for slaughter on a service basis.
  • Internal customers are colleagues who depend on your work: dispatch depends on the chillers being on time; sales depends on accurate stock figures.

Treat internal customers well too. Poor service inside the plant soon becomes poor service to the outside customer.

What customers expect

NeedWhat it means in meat sales and distribution
Right productThe correct grade, cut, weight and packaging
Right quantityExactly what was ordered, no shorts
Right timeDelivered when promised, cold chain intact
Right priceInvoice matches the quotation or price list
Safe and legalInspected product with correct labels and documents
RespectPolite, helpful staff who keep their word

The cost of poor service

An unhappy customer often tells many others. Losing one regular butchery client can mean losing thousands of rand in sales every week. It is far cheaper to keep a customer than to find a new one. Every worker who answers a phone, loads a truck or prepares an order is part of customer service.

lessons.title: Serving customers well
lessons.html:
Good service in practice

Greeting and communicating

  • Greet customers promptly and politely, in person or on the phone. Give your name and the company name.
  • Listen carefully to what they want. Ask questions to clarify: 'Do you want the briskets whole or cut?'
  • Repeat the order back to confirm it.
  • Use clear, simple language and avoid technical jargon unless the customer uses it.
  • Keep promises. If you say you will call back by 14:00, do so.

Taking and processing orders

  1. Record the customer name, account number, contact person and delivery address.
  2. Write product codes, descriptions, quantities and requested weights clearly.
  3. Confirm price and delivery date.
  4. Check stock availability before confirming.
  5. Pass the order to the next step (picking, cutting or dispatch) without delay.

Distribution and delivery

When product leaves the plant, customer service continues:

  • Load according to the delivery route so the first drop is at the back door.
  • Check that the refrigerated truck is at the right temperature before loading, and record it.
  • Check that documents such as the delivery note and invoice match the load.
  • Drivers should be neat, polite and ask the customer to check and sign for the delivery.

Product knowledge

Customers trust staff who know their products. Learn the cuts, grades and pack sizes you sell, how product should be stored and its shelf life. If you do not know an answer, say 'Let me find out for you' and come back with the correct information.

lessons.title: Handling complaints and difficult situations
lessons.html:
Turning a complaint into loyalty

Complaints are a chance to fix a problem and show the customer you care. A complaint handled well can make a customer more loyal than before.

Steps for handling a complaint

  1. Listen without interrupting. Let the customer explain fully.
  2. Acknowledge their feelings: 'I understand you are frustrated that the order arrived late.'
  3. Apologise for the inconvenience, even if it was not your fault personally.
  4. Get the facts: invoice number, product, quantity, date, what exactly is wrong.
  5. Act: solve it within your authority, or refer it to the right person and tell the customer who and when.
  6. Follow up to check the customer is satisfied.
  7. Record the complaint and the action taken.

Common complaints

  • Short delivery or wrong product
  • Product temperature too high on arrival
  • Quality problems such as discolouration or bad smell
  • Invoice errors

For quality or food safety complaints, follow your plant's procedure. The product may need to be quarantined and checked, and the batch traced. Never tell a customer to just use a product that may be unsafe.

Dealing with an angry customer

Stay calm and professional. Do not argue or take it personally. Speak slowly and quietly. Focus on what you can do. If a customer becomes abusive or threatening, call your supervisor.

Learning from complaints

Supervisors should review complaint records regularly. If many complaints are about late deliveries on one route, the route planning may need to change.

Key points

  • External and internal customers both depend on good service.
  • Customers want the right product, quantity, time, price and safe product.
  • Confirm orders by repeating them back and keep your promises.
  • Handle complaints by listening, acknowledging, apologising, acting and following up.
  • Follow the food safety procedure for any quality complaint.
